virals.hook:
🇺🇸🇮🇷 Another war with Iran could put American WARSHIPS directly in the FIRING LINE
 
I caught up with Larry Johnson as reports emerged of another U.S. military buildup in the Middle East, with Israeli officials increasingly expecting Trump to order fresh strikes against Iran.

And Larry thinks Washington is making a potentially catastrophic miscalculation.

He says Iran may have deliberately held back some of its military capabilities during earlier confrontations. But if the U.S. attacks again, he believes Tehran could respond much more aggressively, including attempts to sink American warships.

That's a VERY different war from the short, controlled operation Washington might be hoping for.

We also discussed reports of a highly confidential call between Trump and Netanyahu, Iranian warnings that future retaliation may extend beyond the Persian Gulf, and Senator Chris Murphy's concerns about possible American strikes on civilian infrastructure.

But I pushed Larry on another possibility.

Could Trump be deliberately exaggerating the threat of war to pressure Tehran into accepting a diplomatic deal?

Larry isn't convinced. He sees a president increasingly frustrated by a conflict that has already damaged his political standing, with the midterms just days away.

And the political consequences could extend far beyond Washington.

We discussed Israel's uncertain coalition negotiations, growing American opposition to U.S. support for Israel, and the possibility of a broader regional security realignment involving Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan.

What worries me most is the assumption that Trump can simply order another round of strikes and decide when the fighting stops.

Larry's assessment is that Iran may have other ideas.

And if he's right, the next confrontation could be considerably harder to contain than the last.

virals.name: Matt Burnell
virals.hook:
This is tremendous analysis from @BrettErickson28 as usual.

The Trump Administration's problem is the same as it has always been, it dramatically underestimated Iran's ability and willingness to withstand economic pressure while creating economic pressure of its own. This in spite of constant warnings from within the intelligence community and analysts and researchers focused on Iran. At least the ones that aren't being force-fed their talking points from Israel.

The Islamic Republic of Iran has faced sanctions and economic pressure for all 47 years of its existence. Yes, this is unprecedented levels of economic pressure, but it will take a lot more than a few months of that pressure before Iran really starts feeling it. The Iranian regime has a pain threshold far higher than most in the west can comprehend.

Of course it helps that the Iranian regime does not particularly care how much economic pain its own citizenry feels and that is ultimately why the United States economic war will fail.

There is no doubt Iranian citizens are feeling this far more than the regime is but we are unlikely to ever know the extent of that and historically speaking it is not the poor and hungry that revolt against oppression. The poor and hungry care only about their own survival, not rising up against the oppressors.

Meanwhile, the regime will continue to lean on its considerable offshore assets, efficient military industrial capabilities, and advanced smuggling operations to keep itself afloat until the cost of the fight becomes unsustainable for the United States and its regional partners.

That was ALWAYS the plan for Iran. The Trump Administration has spent this entire conflict talking about how Iran's conventional air and naval forces are obliterated. Iran's air and naval forces are irrelevant. They were for show.

Iran was never going to send a squadron of F-4 Phantoms to bomb US bases or sail a rust bucket of a frigate full of sea cadets to take on the US Navy in the Arabian Sea. The threat was always the asymmetric stuff. Drones, missiles, USVs, UUVs, mines and using those tactics to create unsustainable economic pressure on the region as a whole and no amount of United States military might can defeat that threat. A lesson we should have learned after the last half-century of American warfare.

Now here is the really bad news, if the United States economic war eventually succeeds and the regime cracks, the result will not be an Iran free of oppression and a democratically elected government. It will be an Iran facing civil war.

All three major factions within the Iranian regime will be clawing for control, each with substantial influence within the IRGC. Pro-Iranian militias in Iraq will flood into Iran. There will be separatist movements throughout the country, with conflict spilling over into neighboring countries.

It will be chaos. It will be an economic disaster. It will be a humanitarian disaster. It will irrevocably alter the region. Whether or not it will be altered for the better remains to be seen.

There is something rather extraordinary about the closing days of October, when three dates of profound significance to Iran's history fall within a single week.

And on 31 October, we celebrated the birthday of Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi, whose name has become inseparable from the hopes of many Iranians yearning to reclaim their country.

Nearly twenty-six centuries ago, Cyrus built an empire whose influence extended across much of the ancient world. When he conquered Babylon in 539 BC, he became remembered for restoring religious sanctuaries and permitting displaced peoples to return to their homelands. His legacy would endure in Persian memory and far beyond the borders of his empire.

Centuries later, under the Pahlavi dynasty, Iran underwent another remarkable transformation. Universities expanded, industry developed, infrastructure was modernised, and women gained the right to vote and take their place in the country's political life.

There is a reason Iran's history cannot be reduced to the Islamic Republic.

Long before the first ayatollah claimed authority over the nation, Iran had produced kings, philosophers, poets, mathematicians, architects and physicians whose contributions helped shape human civilisation.

From Persepolis to the poetry of Hafez, from the wisdom of Ferdowsi to the achievements of modern Iranian women, this is a nation whose cultural inheritance belongs among the great treasures of humanity.

And today, as Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi marks another birthday, my hope is that he will soon return to his homeland, answer the calls of those who look to him for leadership, and witness the end of the oppression that has deprived generations of Iranians of their freedoms.

For almost half a century, the Islamic Republic has attempted to bend an ancient civilisation to the will of its rulers. Yet Persian identity, memory and the longing for freedom have endured.

A civilisation that has survived twenty-five centuries of upheaval should never be mistaken for the regime that presently governs it.

May the next chapter of Iran's history be written in freedom, dignity and peace, worthy of the extraordinary people who have sacrificed so much to see their country restored.

Payandeh Iran! Javid Shah!

There is a street in Seoul named after Tehran. The man who proposed that name was executed by the Islamic Republic.

In June 1977, Tehran Mayor Gholamreza Nikpey (غلامرضا نیک‌پی), a close aide of the Shah, visited Seoul. As a symbol of friendship, he proposed that the two cities name streets after each other. Samneung-ro in Gangnam became "Teheran-ro."

On June 27, 1977, Seoul Mayor Koo Ja-choon and Mayor Nikpey attended the naming ceremony together. The memorial stone unveiled that day is inscribed in Korean and Persian: 

"Pledging eternal friendship between the two cities of Seoul and Tehran and their citizens, we name Teheran-ro in Seoul and Seoul Street in Tehran."

At the time, Korea was led by President Park Chung-hee, one of the most respected presidents in Korean history, and Iran by Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, whom many Iranians still remember with deep respect. Both were anti-communist leaders who built up and modernized their nations, and a strong friendship grew between our two peoples.

In August 1977, the Shah appointed Nikpey a senator for his hometown of Isfahan. Javad Shahrestani became the new mayor of Tehran. On November 28, 1977, Tehran named its own "Seoul Street" (خیابان سئول). When Mayor Shahrestani visited Seoul City Hall in October 1978, the Lion and Sun flag stood side by side with the Korean flag at the meeting table.

But 1979 became a tragic year for both nations. In January, the Shah was forced to leave Iran, and the revolution cut this friendship short. On the night of April 10, Nikpey and 10 other former senior officials were tried by a secret revolutionary court, with no lawyer. All were convicted of "corruption on earth" and "war against God," and they were shot by firing squad shortly after 2 a.m. on April 11. Nikpey, the man who built the bridge of friendship between our two cities, was among them. And on October 26, President Park was shot dead by an assassin.

Today, Teheran-ro is the heart of Korea's economy and tech industry. It starts at Gangnam Station, where Koreans march against communism every day. It is the busiest and most vibrant place in all of Korea: Teheran-ro.

Our hope is that Korea will soon take back the liberal democratic government of President Yoon Suk Yeol. May we replace the flag on Teheran-ro with the Lion and Sun, Iran's true flag! And one day, we will walk down Seoul Street in a free Tehran!

Iran will be free, and every Iranian will live each day in safety and happiness! 
We Koreans will do all we can to help a free Iran! Long live free Iran! Javid Shah! 🇮🇷🦁☀️💚🤍❤️
#KingRezaPahlavi‌ForIran #JavidShah 

We pray for a free Iran, for Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi and the Pahlavi family, and for every single person in Iran. 🙏

"Pledging eternal friendship between the two cities of Seoul and Tehran and their citizens..."

outsiders.hook:
🇺🇸🇮🇷 Another war with Iran could put American WARSHIPS directly in the FIRING LINE
 
I caught up with Larry Johnson as reports emerged of another U.S. military buildup in the Middle East, with Israeli officials increasingly expecting Trump to order fresh strikes against Iran.

And Larry thinks Washington is making a potentially catastrophic miscalculation.

He says Iran may have deliberately held back some of its military capabilities during earlier confrontations. But if the U.S. attacks again, he believes Tehran could respond much more aggressively, including attempts to sink American warships.

That's a VERY different war from the short, controlled operation Washington might be hoping for.

We also discussed reports of a highly confidential call between Trump and Netanyahu, Iranian warnings that future retaliation may extend beyond the Persian Gulf, and Senator Chris Murphy's concerns about possible American strikes on civilian infrastructure.

But I pushed Larry on another possibility.

Could Trump be deliberately exaggerating the threat of war to pressure Tehran into accepting a diplomatic deal?

Larry isn't convinced. He sees a president increasingly frustrated by a conflict that has already damaged his political standing, with the midterms just days away.

And the political consequences could extend far beyond Washington.

We discussed Israel's uncertain coalition negotiations, growing American opposition to U.S. support for Israel, and the possibility of a broader regional security realignment involving Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan.

What worries me most is the assumption that Trump can simply order another round of strikes and decide when the fighting stops.

Larry's assessment is that Iran may have other ideas.

And if he's right, the next confrontation could be considerably harder to contain than the last.

outsiders.name: Matt Burnell
outsiders.hook:
This is tremendous analysis from @BrettErickson28 as usual.

The Trump Administration's problem is the same as it has always been, it dramatically underestimated Iran's ability and willingness to withstand economic pressure while creating economic pressure of its own. This in spite of constant warnings from within the intelligence community and analysts and researchers focused on Iran. At least the ones that aren't being force-fed their talking points from Israel.

The Islamic Republic of Iran has faced sanctions and economic pressure for all 47 years of its existence. Yes, this is unprecedented levels of economic pressure, but it will take a lot more than a few months of that pressure before Iran really starts feeling it. The Iranian regime has a pain threshold far higher than most in the west can comprehend.

Of course it helps that the Iranian regime does not particularly care how much economic pain its own citizenry feels and that is ultimately why the United States economic war will fail.

There is no doubt Iranian citizens are feeling this far more than the regime is but we are unlikely to ever know the extent of that and historically speaking it is not the poor and hungry that revolt against oppression. The poor and hungry care only about their own survival, not rising up against the oppressors.

Meanwhile, the regime will continue to lean on its considerable offshore assets, efficient military industrial capabilities, and advanced smuggling operations to keep itself afloat until the cost of the fight becomes unsustainable for the United States and its regional partners.

That was ALWAYS the plan for Iran. The Trump Administration has spent this entire conflict talking about how Iran's conventional air and naval forces are obliterated. Iran's air and naval forces are irrelevant. They were for show.

Iran was never going to send a squadron of F-4 Phantoms to bomb US bases or sail a rust bucket of a frigate full of sea cadets to take on the US Navy in the Arabian Sea. The threat was always the asymmetric stuff. Drones, missiles, USVs, UUVs, mines and using those tactics to create unsustainable economic pressure on the region as a whole and no amount of United States military might can defeat that threat. A lesson we should have learned after the last half-century of American warfare.

Now here is the really bad news, if the United States economic war eventually succeeds and the regime cracks, the result will not be an Iran free of oppression and a democratically elected government. It will be an Iran facing civil war.

All three major factions within the Iranian regime will be clawing for control, each with substantial influence within the IRGC. Pro-Iranian militias in Iraq will flood into Iran. There will be separatist movements throughout the country, with conflict spilling over into neighboring countries.

It will be chaos. It will be an economic disaster. It will be a humanitarian disaster. It will irrevocably alter the region. Whether or not it will be altered for the better remains to be seen.

outsiders.name: Catherine Perez-Shakdam
outsiders.hook:
A CIVILISATION THAT REFUSES TO BE BROKEN

There is something rather extraordinary about the closing days of October, when three dates of profound significance to Iran's history fall within a single week.

On 26 October, we commemorated the birth of His Imperial Majesty Mohammad Reza Shah Pahlavi. On 29 October, Iranians honoured Cyrus the Great, the founder of the Achaemenid Empire. And on 31 October, we celebrated the birthday of Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi, whose name has become inseparable from the hopes of many Iranians yearning to reclaim their country.

Nearly twenty-six centuries ago, Cyrus built an empire whose influence extended across much of the ancient world. When he conquered Babylon in 539 BC, he became remembered for restoring religious sanctuaries and permitting displaced peoples to return to their homelands. His legacy would endure in Persian memory and far beyond the borders of his empire.

Centuries later, under the Pahlavi dynasty, Iran underwent another remarkable transformation. Universities expanded, industry developed, infrastructure was modernised, and women gained the right to vote and take their place in the country's political life.

There is a reason Iran's history cannot be reduced to the Islamic Republic.

Long before the first ayatollah claimed authority over the nation, Iran had produced kings, philosophers, poets, mathematicians, architects and physicians whose contributions helped shape human civilisation.

From Persepolis to the poetry of Hafez, from the wisdom of Ferdowsi to the achievements of modern Iranian women, this is a nation whose cultural inheritance belongs among the great treasures of humanity.

And today, as Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi marks another birthday, my hope is that he will soon return to his homeland, answer the calls of those who look to him for leadership, and witness the end of the oppression that has deprived generations of Iranians of their freedoms.

For almost half a century, the Islamic Republic has attempted to bend an ancient civilisation to the will of its rulers. Yet Persian identity, memory and the longing for freedom have endured.

A civilisation that has survived twenty-five centuries of upheaval should never be mistaken for the regime that presently governs it.

May the next chapter of Iran's history be written in freedom, dignity and peace, worthy of the extraordinary people who have sacrificed so much to see their country restored.

Long live Iran. Long live the Lion and Sun.

Payandeh Iran! Javid Shah!

outsiders.hook:
Teheran-ro: A Street Named Tehran in the Heart of Seoul 🇰🇷🤝🇮🇷🦁☀️💚🤍❤️

There is a street in Seoul named after Tehran. The man who proposed that name was executed by the Islamic Republic.

In June 1977, Tehran Mayor Gholamreza Nikpey (غلامرضا نیک‌پی), a close aide of the Shah, visited Seoul. As a symbol of friendship, he proposed that the two cities name streets after each other. Samneung-ro in Gangnam became "Teheran-ro."

On June 27, 1977, Seoul Mayor Koo Ja-choon and Mayor Nikpey attended the naming ceremony together. The memorial stone unveiled that day is inscribed in Korean and Persian: 

"Pledging eternal friendship between the two cities of Seoul and Tehran and their citizens, we name Teheran-ro in Seoul and Seoul Street in Tehran."

At the time, Korea was led by President Park Chung-hee, one of the most respected presidents in Korean history, and Iran by Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, whom many Iranians still remember with deep respect. Both were anti-communist leaders who built up and modernized their nations, and a strong friendship grew between our two peoples.

In August 1977, the Shah appointed Nikpey a senator for his hometown of Isfahan. Javad Shahrestani became the new mayor of Tehran. On November 28, 1977, Tehran named its own "Seoul Street" (خیابان سئول). When Mayor Shahrestani visited Seoul City Hall in October 1978, the Lion and Sun flag stood side by side with the Korean flag at the meeting table.

But 1979 became a tragic year for both nations. In January, the Shah was forced to leave Iran, and the revolution cut this friendship short. On the night of April 10, Nikpey and 10 other former senior officials were tried by a secret revolutionary court, with no lawyer. All were convicted of "corruption on earth" and "war against God," and they were shot by firing squad shortly after 2 a.m. on April 11. Nikpey, the man who built the bridge of friendship between our two cities, was among them. And on October 26, President Park was shot dead by an assassin.

Today, Teheran-ro is the heart of Korea's economy and tech industry. It starts at Gangnam Station, where Koreans march against communism every day. It is the busiest and most vibrant place in all of Korea: Teheran-ro.

We Koreans have not forgotten our friendship with Pahlavi-era Iran. Yet today, the flag of the Islamic Republic hangs on Teheran-ro. Korea's own government has also been almost completely captured by the Chinese Communist Party. Our hope is that Korea will soon take back the liberal democratic government of President Yoon Suk Yeol. May we replace the flag on Teheran-ro with the Lion and Sun, Iran's true flag! And one day, we will walk down Seoul Street in a free Tehran!

Iran will be free, and every Iranian will live each day in safety and happiness! 
We Koreans will do all we can to help a free Iran! Long live free Iran! Javid Shah! 🇮🇷🦁☀️💚🤍❤️
#KingRezaPahlavi‌ForIran #JavidShah 

We pray for a free Iran, for Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi and the Pahlavi family, and for every single person in Iran. 🙏

"Pledging eternal friendship between the two cities of Seoul and Tehran and their citizens..."

1) Teheran-ro today, near Samseong Station and COEX in Gangnam, the heart of Korea's economy and tech industry.

2) October 16, 1978: Tehran Mayor Javad Shahrestani visits Seoul Mayor Koo Ja-choon at Seoul City Hall. The Korean flag and the Lion and Sun flag stand side by side on the table.

3) June 27, 1977: The naming ceremony of Teheran-ro. The memorial stone reads "Teheran-ro" in Korean and Persian.

4) The same memorial stone today. Behind it hangs the flag of the Islamic Republic. We hope it will be replaced by the Lion and Sun.
